newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN FISHERIES IN FOR REVAMP, SAYS MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN FISHERIES IN FOR REVAMP, SAYS MINISTER.

text.p: South Africa's minister in charge of sea fisheries, Pallo Jordan, said on Friday a policy white paper would be published next month to tackle among other things the question of who should have access to the resource.
"It will enable us during this year to pass legislation to bring about greater equity in the fishing industry," Jordan, minister of environmental affairs and tourism, told reporters.

"We foresee the passage of the new Sea Fisheries Act during the year which will address many of the burning issues that people in the fishing communities and especially historically disadvantaged communities have been bringing (to) the ministry."
Asked if the seafood majors like Sea Harvest Corp Ltd or Irvin and Johnson Ltd had anything to fear from the white paper, Jordan replied:

"There are the inequalities of the past which we are trying to address in the white paper, but at the same time the industry which we have -- mining, manufacturing, fisheries, the rag trade or whatever -- is the industry that you have, and you can't dismantle that callously and without regard to the future of the country.

"They employ large numbers of people and they have the capacity to make that sector internationally competitive... If you just without regard to economic realities begin to take things apart, you might in fact ruin your country," Jordan said.
Black and Coloured (mixed-race) fishing communities have staged repeated protests over the last two years over what they see as the unfair awarding of most fishing quotas to the majors.

"We are also faced with the dangerous situation of escalating poaching, some of it probably morally justified in that people feel deeply aggrieved about inequitable distribution and access to marine resources," Jordan said.
He said abalone were particularly in danger and the government was planning to set up hatcheries so that the shellfish could be restocked in the wild.

"We are actually facing the immediate danger of the depletion of that resource if poaching continues. There is also evidence of the involvement of crime syndicates," Jordan said, without giving further details.
